<reason>Both sides were sharp, but PRO more effectively dismantled CON's load-bearing dilemma ("useless or dangerous"). CON's gaming prong was badly weakened by its own admissions that hidden weights cap farming and that the optimizer's edge "was never knowing ranking exists"; CON's late repair ("state confirmation converts rumor to licensed fact," Google confirmations industrialized SEO) was speculative and somewhat brittle. PRO's credit-score analogy cleanly separated meaning from exploitability, and the regulator-vs-user asymmetry question forced CON into a position (the ranked person is the one party who shouldn't hold the fact) that is hard to defend on a motion about a right to know. CON scored real hits — the exit/competitor challenge exposed PRO's market argument as an IOU, and the "verdict with a middleman"/cookie-banner points kept a live uselessness route — but PRO's forecast-vs-verdict distinction and uncontested premise that users think it's a shuffled deck preserved a genuine informational benefit. CON's "three audiences, three powers" closing was coherent but did not restore the gaming harm. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 and follow-through in [A4.5]/[A5.2]: pinning CON to its concessions that hidden weights cap farming and that knowing ranking exists was never the optimizers' edge, then using the credit-score analogy to show meaning and exploitability are different properties — collapsing CON's central dilemma.</best_rebuttal>
